name: Yoruba religion
areas: the worship of the orishas under Olodumare
most Yoruba are now Christians or Muslims; the orishas are still honoured
Ketu, Sabe and the Yoruba of present-day Benin
Rio de Janeiro and southern Brazil
routes: The Atlantic slave trade carries the orishas to Brazil
Cuban exiles bring Santería to the United States (after 1959)
marks: The sacred city of the Yoruba, where by their tradition the earth was first created; it flourished from around 1000.
The capital of the Oyo Empire, whose kings honoured Shango, the orisha of thunder, remembered as one of their predecessors.
The sacred grove of Osun, goddess of the river; a World Heritage Site since 2005.
Enslaved Yoruba, called Lucumí in Cuba, kept the orishas in Santería (Regla de Ocha).
Casa Branca, one of the first great Candomblé houses, founded by African priestesses in the early 19th century.
A village founded in South Carolina in 1970 to follow Yoruba religion.
The Supreme Court upheld a Santería church's right to practise animal sacrifice here in 1993.
notes: Ile-Ife grows into the sacred city of the Yoruba, centre of the worship of the orishas under Olodumare, the supreme being.
Ile-Ife is at its height; its artists cast naturalistic heads in copper alloy, probably of rulers.
Ifa divination, with its verses of the odu, guides kings and households across the Yoruba kingdoms.
The Oyo Empire rises to dominate the Yoruba lands; its kings honour Shango, the orisha of thunder.
Through the Atlantic slave trade, enslaved Yoruba carry the orishas to Brazil and the Caribbean.
The collapse of the Oyo Empire (1830s) and the wars that follow send many enslaved Yoruba to Cuba and Brazil, where Santería and Candomblé take shape; at home Islam and Christianity spread.
Most Yoruba become Christians or Muslims; Cuban exiles bring Santería to the United States, and Candomblé grows across Brazil.
UNESCO proclaims Ifa divination a masterpiece of humanity's oral heritage (2005) and the sacred grove of Osogbo becomes a World Heritage Site; the orishas are honoured across the Americas.
src: J. D. Y. Peel, Christianity, Islam, and Oriṣa Religion (2016)
